title: Images and Layers
subtitle: How Docker's union filesystem makes images fast, small, and shareable

content.text: A Docker image is not a single monolithic file — it's a stack of read-only layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. When you run a container, Docker adds one thin writable layer on top. This design means: layers are cached and reused across images; if 10 images share the same base OS layer, that layer is stored once on disk; and downloading a new image only transfers the layers you don't already have.

content.code:
# See the layers of any image
docker history node:20-alpine
# IMAGE          CREATED       CREATED BY                      SIZE
# 1d46ed2a75d7   3 weeks ago   CMD ["node"]                    0B
# <missing>      3 weeks ago   ENV NODE_VERSION=20.11.0        0B
# <missing>      3 weeks ago   RUN /bin/sh -c apk add --no-… 44.3MB
# <missing>      3 weeks ago   RUN /bin/sh -c apk update      3.1MB
# <missing>      3 weeks ago   /bin/sh -c #(nop) ADD file:… 7.38MB
# Each line = one layer. Sizes add up to the total image size.

# Show detailed image info including all layers
docker inspect node:20-alpine | grep -A5 'Layers'

content.text: The first line of every Dockerfile is FROM <base-image>. Your choice has a huge impact on image size, security surface, and build speed. The most important variants to know:

items: node:20 — full Debian-based image. ~1 GB. Has everything, but huge. Avoid in production.
node:20-slim — stripped Debian. ~220 MB. Good balance for Node apps.
node:20-alpine — Alpine Linux base. ~55 MB. Minimal, fast to pull, preferred for production. Uses musl libc instead of glibc — rare compatibility issues.
scratch — empty base (literally nothing). Used for Go or Rust apps that compile to a fully static binary.

content.code:
docker pull node:20        && docker images node:20
# node   20        ~1.1GB

docker pull node:20-slim   && docker images node:20-slim
# node   20-slim   ~220MB

docker pull node:20-alpine && docker images node:20-alpine
# node   20-alpine  ~55MB

# Rule of thumb: start with alpine, switch to slim if you hit issues

content.text: Layer caching — the build speed secret

Docker caches each layer. When you rebuild an image, Docker reuses cached layers until it finds one that changed — then rebuilds from that point down. This is why the order of instructions in your Dockerfile matters enormously for build speed.

content.code:
# ❌ SLOW — copies code first, so npm install reruns on every code change
FROM node:20-alpine
COPY . .               # copies ALL files — cache busted on any change
RUN npm install        # reruns every time any file changes
CMD ["node", "app.js"]

# ✅ FAST — copies package.json first; npm install only reruns when deps change
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./  # only package files — cache busted only when deps change
RUN npm install        # cached unless package.json changed
COPY . .               # copy source code last
CMD ["node", "app.js"]

# With the fast version:
# First build: all layers run (slow)
# Code change only: only last COPY . . and CMD rerun (fast)
# Dep change: npm install and below rerun

content.text: Pin your base image versions. Always use node:20-alpine not node:alpine (which is 'latest alpine' and changes over time). Pinning ensures reproducible builds — the same image is built months later. For critical production systems, pin to the full digest: node:20-alpine@sha256:...

questions.question: You have a Dockerfile that runs COPY . . then RUN npm install. You change a single source file and rebuild. What happens?
options: Only the changed file is rebuilt — Docker diffs the filesystem
The COPY layer cache is busted, so npm install reruns too — even though package.json didn't change
Nothing changes because Docker detects npm install already ran
Docker skips COPY and only reruns npm install
questions.explanation: COPY . . copies everything including your changed source file, so that layer's cache is invalidated. Every layer AFTER a cache miss also reruns — including RUN npm install. This is why you should always COPY package*.json first, run npm install, then COPY the rest of the source.

faq.a: Like .gitignore but for Docker builds. A .dockerignore file tells Docker which files to exclude from the build context (what gets sent to the Docker daemon). Always exclude node_modules, .git, .env, and large binary files. Example: add 'node_modules' and '.git' and '*.log' to .dockerignore to dramatically speed up builds.

examples: Switching a Node.js app from node:20 to node:20-alpine cuts the image from 1.1 GB to ~150 MB with the app included — 7× smaller, faster to push/pull in CI
Proper layer ordering can cut CI build time from 3 minutes to 15 seconds by avoiding npm install on every code change
